title: Diagnosing Connectivity, Layer by Layer
intro: When something is 'unreachable', you check connectivity in layers: can I resolve the name, can I reach the port, does the app actually respond.

steps.prompt: Check if the hostname resolves at all.
steps.explanation: If this step fails, the problem is DNS, not the app — always check this first, it rules out an entire category of causes.
steps.why: 'dig +short' prints just the IP with none of the extra query/answer-section noise a plain 'dig' dumps — faster to read at a glance during an incident when you just need the one value.

steps.prompt: DNS resolves fine. Now check if the port is even reachable.
steps.explanation: This confirms something is listening on that port — separate from whether the application logic actually works correctly.
steps.why: -z tells nc to just test the connection and exit instead of opening an interactive session, and -v prints the result — without -z you'd be dropped into a raw socket session, which isn't what you want for a quick health check.

steps.prompt: Port's open. Now check the actual HTTP response.
steps.explanation: A 200 here means DNS, network, and application are all fine — three layers confirmed in three commands.
steps.why: -I sends a HEAD request and shows just the response headers, which is enough to confirm the app is actually answering — -v is the heavier option, useful when you need the full TLS handshake and connection details, not just the final status.

steps.prompt: Check how long the request actually took (useful when 'slow' is the complaint, not 'broken').
steps.explanation: This isolates total request time without downloading/printing the response body — handy for quick latency checks in scripts.
steps.why: -o /dev/null discards the body and -s suppresses curl's own progress output, leaving only the -w formatted timing value — without those two flags this command would dump the entire response onto your screen just to show one number at the end.
